**Technical note 6/6: Evaluate discovery, effort, and model components**

Compare the current VRChat system with non-personalized popularity and rating priors. Then test a shared content-and-history model, add collaborative world embeddings, and finally add limited user-specific parameters. Test each action type with and without it, and fixed versus learned contributions. A fixed rule's failure does not establish that trained hybrids fail; a hybrid still needs to demonstrate its benefit.

Evaluate candidate generation by whether it retrieves items later receiving positive feedback. Compare rankers using the same candidate sets. Then test the complete system. Recall based only on observed ratings is incomplete. Unobserved items are not confirmed unsuitable items.

Measure actions and time from display to a new-world visit, and the proportion of users making a new-world visit in a fixed period. Keep non-visitors and nonrespondents in the relevant denominator. A fast visit does not prove satisfaction.

Record clicks, actual visits, repeated visits, duration, response rates, and feedback separately. A story or exhibition may be satisfying after one visit. Check users with zero, one, or few prior ratings; permanent nonrespondents; new or rarely rated worlds; uncommon tastes; and multiple interests. Preserve diversity and opportunities for compatible new worlds.

For zero/one/ten-rating tests, keep users and candidates fixed. A nested sample can use the first rating in the same sequence for the one-rating condition and the first ten for the ten-rating condition.

Seeds do not create new independent users. For a user-level paired bootstrap, first average each user's metric across seeds. Calculate each user's paired difference, then resample users with replacement, retaining both methods. Declare resample count, seed, and interval method.

An interval for residual-minus-raw transfer is not an interval for residual-minus-prior. Including zero does not prove equivalence. Report both Liked@5 and Not for me@5, and Utility@5 for the chosen lambda.

Also test whether "Not for me" changes recommendations appropriately, without rejecting a broad group of tags. Responsiveness is a separate concern: [Wang et al. (2023), Learning from Negative User Feedback and Measuring Responsiveness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.12256).

**Technical note 5/6: Baselines and supporting research**

Please keep these comparison methods distinct:

- Non-personalized popularity: counts such as saves or visits, not personal satisfaction.

- Non-personalized item-level rating prior: other users' ratings, without the target user's history.

- Item-based collaborative filtering: the person's history and collaborative item relationships. It can personalize recommendations.

- Content-based recommendation: content and personal history; can cover new worlds but may transfer broad features poorly.

- Implicit-feedback ALS/BPR: action patterns; useful for candidates, but action prediction is not satisfaction prediction.

- Shared hybrid: typed history, content, and collaborative information; an unproven candidate here.

- Large multi-behavior/sequential model: more history and order; not an automatic solution to different action meanings.

Item-based CF: [Sarwar et al. (2001)](https://experts.umn.edu/en/publications/item-based-collaborative-filtering-recommendation-algorithms/).

Implicit methods should not all be described as treating every unobserved item as a confirmed dislike: [Hu et al. (2008)](https://yifanhu.net/PUB/cf.pdf), [Rendle et al., BPR (UAI 2009; arXiv deposit 2012)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1205.2618).

Research on Twitter Favorites found several motives, including differences within one person's behavior: [Meier et al. (2014)](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/ICWSM/article/view/14541). It did not measure VRChat users' motives.

Shortlists provided useful recommendation information, but predicted the movie finally chosen, not satisfaction after watching. A finer distinction between examined and saved items did not significantly improve prediction: [Schnabel et al. (2016), Section 4.3/Table 9](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/using-shortlists-support-decision-making-improve-recommender-system-performance/).

RMBRec reports TMall NDCG@10 of 0.0838 with all behaviors and 0.1043 without add-to-cart. The same removal reduced performance on two other datasets: [Cai et al. (2026), Table 3](https://arxiv.org/html/2601.08705v3). This is a reported result from another domain, not a VRChat result or independent verification of that difference's statistical significance. Test each behavior's value rather than always adding or removing it.

**Technical note 4/6: Training without future information**

A possible training objective is:

```

Loss = -sum_e in E_T omega_e * log p_hat(r_e | X_at_t_rec)

       + alpha * ||parameters||^2

omega_e >= 0; alpha >= 0

```

E_T contains eligible training examples available at training cutoff T. Each links a user, world, recommendation, and valid feedback. X_at_t_rec is the information available just before the recommendation. Repeated edits are not independent votes. "Not for me" is a category, not a negative sample weight.

1. At recommendation time, record candidates, positions, model version, and features or a reproducible snapshot ID.

2. For training, reconstruct inputs available at recommendation time. For temporal evaluation, use a model trained only on data available before the evaluation cutoff.

3. Link a later confirmed visit using a declared attribution rule and time window.

4. Link voluntary feedback when the relationship to that visit is reliable. Keep its value and submission time; exclude unrelated later visits.

5. At cutoff T, use only feedback and edits already available. Keep the input frozen at recommendation time, not feedback-submission time.

6. Exclude ambiguous attribution from that event-based evaluation or report it separately. Decide the rule before inspecting test results.

The later visit, duration, and Favorite may be outcomes. They must not enter the earlier input. A later rating can be the intended target without making its consequences valid earlier features.

Current state has at most one valid response per user-world pair. An edit replaces it; cancellation removes it, rather than making it neutral.

Historical tests must use the state known then. A positive response at time 4, negative edit at 6, and cancellation at 8 means positive at 5, negative at 7, and unanswered at 9. Today's latest state cannot replace all past states. Declare training cutoffs and outcome windows separately.

In temporal evaluation, apply the cutoff to other users' ratings, item priors, collaborative embeddings, and world updates. A per-user split alone does not exclude other users' future records.

Using only actual responses avoids invented labels. It does not remove response-selection bias. Nonnegative weights need justified assumptions before they can correct bias.

[Schnabel et al. (2016), Recommendations as Treatments](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v48/schnabel16.html)

**Technical note 3/6: Three outcomes, two outcomes, and utility**

For three outcomes, use utilities +1, 0, and -lambda:

```

s = p_plus - lambda*p_minus

lambda >= 0

```

Zero is the chosen utility for "It was okay." It does not claim equal psychological distances between choices. The penalty requires testing.

Example distributions are ordered as (Liked it, It was okay, Not for me). At lambda=0.5:

- User A, scenic world: (0.70, 0.20, 0.10), score 0.650.

- User A, cooperative game: (0.35, 0.40, 0.25), score 0.225.

- User B, scenic world: (0.25, 0.50, 0.25), score 0.125.

- User B, cooperative game: (0.65, 0.20, 0.15), score 0.575.

For A's scenic candidate: 0.70 - 0.5*0.10 = 0.65. The same candidates have different orders for A and B. These are hypothetical values, not trained predictions.

Changing lambda can change a three-outcome ranking. For candidates A=(0.6,0.3,0.1) and B=(0.7,0.0,0.3), B ranks higher at lambda=0, but A ranks higher at lambda=1.

For two exhaustive outcomes:

```

p_minus = 1-p_plus

s = (1+lambda)*p_plus-lambda

```

A common nonnegative lambda leaves the order unchanged, including ties. This also applies to a user-specific lambda that is constant across that user's candidates. A threshold s>0 means p_plus>lambda/(1+lambda), so changing lambda can change which candidates qualify. It can also matter when combined with another objective, but not in a pure top-K ranking by this binary score.

Unanswered feedback remains missing in both designs. Predictions from voluntary responses are not automatically calibrated satisfaction probabilities for everyone.

For five ranked items with observed test labels:

```

Liked@5 = count("Liked it" in top 5) / 5

Not for me@5 = count("Not for me" in top 5) / 5

Utility@5 = Liked@5 - lambda*Not for me@5

```

Use proportions in Utility@5. Specify the treatment of fewer than five candidates in advance. Missing VRChat feedback must not become zero utility. Report response rates and denominators separately.

**Technical note 2/6: Fixed similarity transfer and residual transfer**

Let J_u contain distinct worlds with valid feedback before recommendation time. mu_w is a non-personalized item-level rating prior based on other users. Define:

```

y_uj in {-1, 0, +1}

K(w,j) >= 0; a_uj >= 0; tau_K > 0

h_uwj = a_uj * K(w,j)

D_uw = tau_K + sum_j h_uwj

s_raw = (tau_K*mu_w + sum_j h_uwj*y_uj) / D_uw

s_residual = mu_w + sum_j h_uwj*(y_uj-mu_j) / D_uw

```

a_uj is an optional observation weight. Use the same effective weight in numerator and denominator. Setting a_uj=1 gives equal additional observation weights. Signed similarities, such as a negative embedding cosine, need a separately defined treatment.

If mu_w and y are in [-1,1], the raw score is a weighted average in that range. With no observations, both rules return mu_w.

For the same history, weights, and tau_K:

```

s_residual - s_raw

  = sum_j h_uwj*(mu_w-mu_j) / D_uw

```

This follows by writing mu_w over D_uw and subtracting the raw numerator. The y terms cancel.

For mu_w=0.8, mu_j=0, y_uj=0, and K=tau_K=a=1, the raw score is 0.4 and the residual score is 0.8. A neutral response to a generally neutral item does not lower the other candidate's prior in the residual rule. This example is not evidence that it predicts better.

Residual scores are not bounded by [-1,1]. With mu_w=1, mu_j=-1, y_uj=1, and K=tau_K=a=1, the result is 2. Treat it as a ranking score, not a probability.

A three-category pseudo-count interpretation requires prior probabilities pi_w,k that sum to 1, with mu_w=pi_w,+ - pi_w,-:

```

q_k = (tau_K*pi_w,k + sum_j h_uwj*I(y_uj=k)) / D_uw

s_raw = q_plus - q_minus

```

I(condition) is 1 when true and 0 otherwise. mu_w alone cannot recover all three prior probabilities. Transferred ratings are pseudo-observations, not independent ratings of the candidate itself. Large similarity totals do not establish equivalent confidence. Calibration is still needed.

Neither rule guarantees better recommendations.

**Technical note 1/6: Shared model and cold-start limits**

An illustrative model is:

```

v_w = e_w + B * x_w

z_k = b_k + b_wk + f_k(v_w, H_u(<t), c)

      + g(n_u) * dot(p_uk, v_w)

p_hat_k = softmax_k(z)

g(n) = n / (n + tau_U), tau_U > 0

```

x_w is world content, such as descriptions and tags. e_w is a world-ID representation learned from other users' reactions. B maps content into that representation. H_u(<t) is history available before recommendation time, with action types kept separate. f_k is shared across users and can represent several interests. p_uk is a user-specific adjustment. n_u counts valid ratings of distinct worlds; editing a rating does not increase it. The b terms are biases, c is available context, and k is the feedback category.

When n_u=0, g(0)=0 removes only the user-specific term. The shared f_k can still produce different predictions from different histories. Keep three claims separate: prediction is possible; accuracy improves; it works for people who never submit feedback. Only the first follows from the architecture. Hiding ratings from people who normally rate does not fully test permanent nonrespondents.

The gate controls only the user-specific term. The shared history model also needs sensitivity tests and regularization. Compare the same history with and without one positive, neutral, or negative response. Check the rated world, close candidates, and unrelated candidates. Repeat for edits and cancellations. Regularize both shared and user-specific parameters.

Many ratings in one genre do not establish confidence in another. For new worlds, use zero or declared priors for untrained world-ID embeddings and biases. Content can provide an initial representation. With no informative personal history, begin with varied compatible candidates.

Without post-visit labels across the service, this supervised output cannot yet be trained. Compare with existing recommendations as optional feedback accumulates. A small regularized model can be tested first; a large neural model is not required.

LightFM is a reference for combining metadata and collaborative information. This history model and three-category output are not an exact implementation or a tested extension of LightFM.

[Kula (2015), Metadata Embeddings for User and Item Cold-start Recommendations](https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.08439)

details:
**Summary**

Help each user discover suitable worlds they have not visited, with less effort.

Learn from normal browsing, Favorites, and visits, even when the user never submits ratings.

Keep Favorites unchanged and use optional feedback after a visit as an additional signal.

The [For You summary](https://ask.vrchat.com/t/may-29-developer-stream-q-a-summary/48500) describes a personalized experiment. The [world rating announcement](https://ask.vrchat.com/t/where-were-landing-on-ai-in-vrchat/49178/1) describes planned thumbs-up/down feedback. These sources do not specify the internal model or training labels. I am not claiming a defect in the current system.

**1. Keep Favorites useful before and after visits**

A Favorite may mean "visit later," a friend's suggestion, a useful meeting place, or a world the user enjoyed. I would like to keep all these uses. Saving a world does not establish that the user visited or enjoyed it.

Saved but unvisited worlds should remain eligible for discovery recommendations.

Long or repeated visits may reflect conversation, being AFK, home worlds, events, or joining friends. Saves, visits, time spent, and explicit feedback should remain distinct. Missing feedback should not be treated as a neutral or negative rating.

**2. Personalize through normal use, not required ratings**

A shared model could combine world content, patterns in other users' reactions, and each person's browsing, saving, and visit history. The goal is to personalize recommendations even for people who never submit ratings. Optional post-visit feedback would provide an additional signal.

For example, someone who saves scenic worlds and cooperative games should discover unfamiliar worlds in both categories, even if they never submit a rating. Do not reduce all Favorites to one average interest or require an initial questionnaire.

Generate candidates from several interests, collaborative relationships, and new worlds. Respect platform compatibility and content settings. World content can provide an initial basis for recommending new worlds. With no useful personal history, begin with varied compatible worlds.

This architecture can produce personal predictions without prior ratings. Whether it improves recommendations, especially for people who never rate, still needs evaluation.

**3. Avoid simple rules that misread behavior**

Treating every Favorite as a positive rating confuses saving with satisfaction. Broad content tags can also transfer a few reactions too strongly to other worlds. A single negative response should not permanently hide a world or reject its whole genre.

Keeping action types separate does not guarantee better predictions. More behavior types or a larger model do not guarantee improvement either. Both shared learning and user-specific adjustments need tests for overreaction to limited feedback.

**4. Test discovery and effort, not only engagement**

Compare the approach with current recommendations, non-personalized baselines, content-based methods, and collaborative filtering. Test the value of shared history, collaborative world features, and user-specific adjustments separately. Evaluate candidate generation and ranking separately, then the complete system.

Measure actions and time to a new-world visit, visit rates, response rates, and feedback separately. Keep non-visitors and nonrespondents in the relevant denominators. A quick visit does not prove satisfaction. A story or exhibition can be satisfying after one visit.

Check new worlds, uncommon interests, multiple interests, and users with few or no ratings. Preserve diversity and opportunities to discover compatible new worlds. Use information available at recommendation time, without adding later visits, saves, or rating edits to earlier inputs. Voluntary respondents do not represent all users.

**This is a proposal to test against VRChat's existing recommendations; its benefits would need to be evaluated.**

**5. Keep post-visit feedback optional**

Feedback should be voluntary and available only after an actual visit, without repeated prompts. UI details can remain with VRChat.

"Liked it / It was okay / Not for me" is an illustrative alternative, not the announced thumbs-up/down interface. Saving, visiting, and explicit feedback can also remain separate in a two-choice system.

Optional numbered comments provide model examples, formulas, failure cases, references, and evaluation details.
title: Personalized world discovery from normal use and optional post-visit feedback
